title: Movie Recommendation System
summary: A content based movie recommendation app that helps users discover their next favourite film by analysing movie metadata and finding similar titles using TF-IDF and cosine similarity.
points: How to use the app. Select a movie from the searchable dropdown and click Find Similar Movies. The app returns five recommendations based on the selected film, with movie posters to make browsing easier.

Dataset and data source. Used the TMDB 5000 Movies and TMDB 5000 Credits datasets, commonly available through Kaggle. The movies dataset provides information such as genres, keywords, overview and title, while the credits dataset contains cast and crew details.

Data preprocessing. Loaded both CSV files with Pandas and merged them using the movie title. Parsed the genres, keywords, cast and crew fields from their stored JSON-like format, selected relevant names and combined useful metadata into a single feature for each movie.

Feature engineering. Cleaned the combined text and joined selected movie attributes into a single content description. This helps the system compare movies using information about their content rather than relying on user ratings or viewing history.

TF-IDF vectorization. Used Scikit-learn's TfidfVectorizer to convert the combined movie descriptions into numerical vectors. TF-IDF gives more importance to informative terms and less importance to terms that appear frequently across many movies.
Cosine similarity. Calculated cosine similarity between the movie vectors to measure how closely their content matches. Higher similarity scores indicate movies with more similar metadata.

Recommendation process. Stored the similarity matrix and mapped each movie title to its dataset index. When a user selects a movie, the app retrieves its similarity scores, ranks other movies from highest to lowest and displays the top five recommendations.

Poster integration and deployment. Used the TMDB API to fetch movie posters using movie IDs and displayed the results in a Streamlit interface. Deployed the application online so users can try the recommendation system without running the notebook.

title: SMS Spam Detection
summary: A machine learning project that detects spam messages using natural language processing, TF-IDF and a Linear SVM model. The application helps users identify unwanted messages through a simple web interface.
points: Problem statement. Spam messages often contain fake offers, unwanted advertisements and suspicious links. The goal of this project is to build a machine learning model that can automatically identify whether a message is spam or a normal message called ham.

Dataset preparation. Used a labeled SMS dataset containing messages and their categories. Loaded the data using Pandas and selected the required columns for training. This gave the model examples of both spam and legitimate messages to learn from.

Text preprocessing. Cleaned the messages by converting text to lowercase and removing unwanted characters and links. For example, WIN a FREE prize becomes win a free prize. This helps keep the text consistent before converting it into numerical features.

Train and test split. Divided the dataset into training and testing sets using an 80 to 20 ratio. The training data helps the model learn patterns, while the testing data checks how well it predicts messages it has not seen before.

TF-IDF feature extraction. Used TF-IDF to convert text messages into numerical values that a machine learning model can understand. It gives more importance to useful words and less importance to words that appear frequently across messages. This helps the model identify patterns commonly associated with spam.

Model training. Used a Linear Support Vector Machine, also called Linear SVM, to classify messages as spam or ham. The model learns from the TF-IDF features and finds patterns that help separate the two categories.

Model evaluation. Evaluated the model using accuracy, precision, recall and F1-score. Accuracy measures overall correctness, precision checks how reliable spam predictions are, and recall measures how many actual spam messages are detected. The confusion matrix helps identify incorrect predictions.
Model saving. Saved the trained TF-IDF and Linear SVM pipeline using Pickle. This allows the application to reuse the trained model without repeating the entire training process.

Streamlit application. Built a simple web interface using Streamlit where users can enter a message and check its category. The saved model processes the message and displays whether it is spam or ham.

Results and conclusion. The model achieved 98.39% accuracy on the evaluation dataset, with 99.25% precision, 88.59% recall and a 93.62% F1-score. The project demonstrates how NLP and machine learning can be used to detect spam messages and make predictions through a web application.

title: Bank Customer Churn Prediction & Retention Analytics
summary: An end-to-end machine learning project that predicts bank customer attrition by analyzing customer demographics, banking relationships, credit information and transaction behavior. Built using Scikit-learn and Gradient Boosting, the project includes data analysis, preprocessing pipelines, model comparison, hyperparameter tuning and an interactive Streamlit application for identifying customers at risk of leaving.
points: Problem statement. Customer attrition is an important challenge for banking institutions because losing existing customers can affect business growth and revenue. The goal of this project is to build a machine learning system that identifies customers who are likely to leave by analyzing their banking activities, account details and transaction behavior.

Dataset collection and understanding. Used a Bank Customer Churn dataset containing 10,127 customer records and 23 original columns. The dataset includes demographic information, education, income category, card category, account relationships, credit limits and transaction details. Identified Attrition_Flag as the target variable for predicting whether a customer is existing or attrited.

Data inspection and quality checks. Examined dataset dimensions, column names, data types, missing values and duplicate records. Checked the target distribution and verified the available features. The initial missing-value checks showed no missing values in the examined columns.

Data cleaning and feature selection. Removed CLIENTNUM because it is a customer identifier rather than a meaningful predictive feature. Also removed the two Naive Bayes classifier output columns to prevent target leakage. Prepared the cleaned dataset with 19 input features and one target variable, resulting in 10,127 records.

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA). Analyzed customer attrition distribution and explored relationships between customer demographics, banking activities and churn. Used Pandas, Matplotlib and Seaborn to examine distributions, compare customer groups and understand patterns in the dataset.

Customer behavior analysis. Compared existing and attrited customers using important numerical features. Observed that attrited customers had lower average transaction amounts, fewer transactions, higher inactive months and fewer banking product relationships. For example, average transaction count was approximately 44.93 for attrited customers compared with 68.67 for existing customers.

Target variable preparation. Converted the Attrition_Flag into a binary classification target, separating existing customers and attrited customers. Examined the class distribution, which contained 8,500 existing customers and 1,627 attrited customers. Recognized the class imbalance while evaluating model performance.

Data preprocessing pipeline. Separated numerical and categorical features using Scikit-learn. Applied median imputation and StandardScaler to numerical columns, while categorical columns were processed using most-frequent imputation and OneHotEncoder with handle_unknown='ignore'. Combined these transformations using ColumnTransformer to maintain consistent preprocessing.

Train-test splitting. Divided the dataset into training and testing subsets to evaluate the model on unseen customer records. Kept preprocessing inside the machine learning pipeline to avoid data leakage and ensure consistent transformations during training and prediction.

Model development and comparison. Implemented and compared multiple classification algorithms, including Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, Extra Trees and Gradient Boosting. Evaluated their performance using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score and ROC-AUC to identify a suitable model for customer attrition prediction.

Model selection. Selected Gradient Boosting as the preferred model based on its predictive performance. Gradient Boosting builds an ensemble of decision trees sequentially, where each new tree helps correct errors made by previous trees. This approach provided strong classification performance on the customer churn dataset.

Hyperparameter optimization. Applied GridSearchCV with 5-fold cross-validation to improve the Gradient Boosting model. Tested 16 parameter combinations across 80 model fits. The best configuration used learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=3, min_samples_leaf=5 and n_estimators=150, achieving a best cross-validation recall of approximately 86.94%.

Model evaluation. Evaluated the tuned model on the unseen test dataset using a confusion matrix, classification report and ROC-AUC score. Achieved 96.79% accuracy, 96.76% precision, 82.77% recall, 89.22% F1-score and 99.05% ROC-AUC. These metrics demonstrate strong overall classification performance while highlighting the importance of detecting attrited customers.

Feature importance analysis. Used Gradient Boosting feature importance to understand which customer attributes contributed most to model predictions. This helps identify relevant customer behavior patterns and provides insights that can support data-driven retention strategies.

Model serialization. Saved the trained machine learning pipeline using Joblib so the application can reuse the fitted preprocessing transformations and Gradient Boosting model without repeating the training process. This also helps maintain consistency between training and deployment.

Streamlit application development. Developed an interactive web application using Streamlit that allows users to enter customer details such as age, income category, credit limit, inactive months, transaction activity and account relationships. The application uses the saved model to generate customer attrition predictions.

Prediction and risk identification. Integrated the trained pipeline into the application to process user inputs and predict whether a customer is likely to remain or become attrited. Displayed the prediction in a simple and understandable format to demonstrate how machine learning can assist customer retention analysis.

Results and conclusion. Successfully developed an end-to-end customer churn prediction workflow, from raw dataset exploration and preprocessing to model optimization and application deployment. The project demonstrates how machine learning can help banking institutions identify potentially at-risk customers and make more informed customer retention decisions.
